#4784. 23 dazzling panoramic images from the 2026 Epson International Pano Awards

Published Oct 25, 2026 1:08 PM EDT

When limited to a 3:2 aspect, your photographs can miss the full beauty of a place. Panoramic photos capture whole landscapes, sweeping cityscapes, and the entirety of a night’s sky.

The Epson International Pano Awards celebrate the huge beauty of panoramic with stunning images from Chile to Iceland and New Zealand to New York City. Landscape and aerial Photographer Daniel Viñé Garcia of Spain took top honors as the Open Photographer of the Year for a beautiful photo (seen below) at the Parinacota Volcano in Chile.

“Parinacota Volcano was one of the main photographic goals of my trip to Chile,” Garcia said in a statement. “Rising to more than 6,300 metres, its distinctive snow-covered cone has an almost perfect symmetry that immediately reminded me of volcanoes such as Mount Fuji. Beside it stands Pomerape, another giant reaching more than 6,200 metres, together forming one of the most impressive landscapes I encountered during the journey. After allowing time for proper acclimatization, I spent three days and three nights at around 4,500 metres above sea level, giving myself the best possible chance of photographing the area under ideal conditions.”

“This image was captured during the final moments of sunset. After one last burst of light, the landscape gradually took on magenta tones, wrapping the volcanoes and the high-altitude lakes in a particularly special atmosphere. The original capture was a 360-degree aerial panorama made from 33 individual exposures. I later refined the framing from the full panorama to concentrate the final composition on the volcanoes, the light, and the shapes of the landscape,” he concluded.

This year’s competition drew 4,084 entries from photographers in 93 countries.

You can find the full set of 2026 winning and runner-up photographs on the Epson International Pano Awards website.

#4783. Volkswagen’s new electric Jetta offers 285 miles of range for under $12K

Volkswagen is offering its Chinese-market Jetta M6 electric sedan with nearly 290 miles of CLTC-rated range for less than $12,000 (USD), and if that’s not what “der people’s wagen” should be all about, I don’t know what is.

Launched as a joint venture between FAW and Volkswagen Group, the Jetta brand’s first battery electric car is finally here – and it is a genuinely accessible, capable, and kinda decent-looking family sedan in the same way VW’s original Type I was when it was first developed in the 1940s.

The new Jetta M6 was launched earlier this in three variants: the 465 Pro, 555 Max and 555 Ultra; each priced at 79,800 yuan (~$11,800), 89,800 yuan and 99,800 yuan, respectively, with the model numbers corresponding to the car’s estimated CLTC range in kilometers (which maths out around ~285 and 345 miles, if you’re curious).

Built on FAW’s Jiesi architecture, the M6 measures 4,806 mm long and 1,868 mm wide, putting it right in that sedan sweet spot between the Civic/Corolla and Accord/Camry crews, and within a few mm this way and that of the Tesla Model 3, so it should have plenty of room for young professionals and families – but the M6′ real selling point is its tech.

Inside, the Jetta M6 offers an 8.88″ driver display along with a big 15.6″ central touchscreen that integrates Chinese AI assistants Doubao and DeepSeek and ships with Apple CarPlay baked in. Advanced ADAS with, “intelligent cruise assistance, automatic emergency braking, and automated parking” is standard.

The entry-level “465 Pro” version of the Jetta M6 comes equipped with 42.9 kWh LFP battery and a 113 kW (~150 hp) electric motor driving the front wheels, a combination the company says is good for a 8.3-second sprint to 100 km/h (62 mph). Stepping up to the 555 versions gets you a larger 51.9 kWh battery and more powerful 145 kW (~195 hp) motor that cuts that sprint to 6.8 seconds.

Both the 42.9 and 51.0 kWh batteries are lithium iron phosphate deals supplied by CALB, with charging from 20% to 80% taking about 30 minutes.

There are parts of the US where a car like this would be perfect -- it's got enough range for the daily commute and short weekend day trips. Not for everyone, but for enough people that it would be a big deal.

Would those features and performance numbers be enough to get you to look at something like this in the US, even at twice the price? It seems to me that North America’s VW dealers need all the help they can get, and a volume leader like this with a “back to basics” ad campaign that plays on a different kind of nostalgia – nostalgia for a time when people could afford a Jetta, maybe? – could be a winner. Let us know what you think in the comments.

#4782. The GFG Style Peralta D Is a Maserati-Based Grand Tourer Rebodied in Actual Copper

The Fabrizio Giugiaro-penned one-off is inspired by his father Giorgetto’s iconic work in the late 1960s and 1970s.

Legendary car designer Giorgetto Giugiaro founded GFG Style with his son Fabrizio after leaving Italdesign Giugiaro over a decade ago. The studio has kept busy since then with work on concepts, design studies, and even one-offs, the latest of which blends elements of some of Giorgetto’s most famous designs with an unusual material: unpainted copper.

This one-off is the GFG Style Peralta D, a Fabrizio Giugiaro-penned 2+2 grand tourer that plays the hits with a wedge shape and a glassy canopy that can be opened either as exceptionally small gullwing doors or as one massive single piece. GFG Style calls this an evolution of the “dome” design used on the previous Peralta S one-off, and it gets even more unusual at the back of the car. Here, two more gullwing sections open up like the engine cover on the elder Giugiaro’s DeTomaso Mangusta design to allow rear passengers to enter and exit ... provided they can contort themselves through the diagonal opening created by the combined moving roof and rear panels.

The lower section of that roof, like the rest of what sits under the beltline, is made of bare copper. This creates a rich reddish surface now, although it is one that would presumably be susceptible to the same surface oxidation that develops over the metal that turned the Statue of Liberty green over time. Carbon fiber elements do exist along the front and rear bumpers, but these are relatively hidden. That leaves just the extensive copper brightwork, the reflective glass, and areas of more muted black trim to define the look of the car.

All that copper conceals what GFG Style calls “an aluminum chassis and top-of-the-line mechanical components based on the Maserati GranTurismo.” As both the current V-6 GranTurismo and its V-8 predecessor are themselves built around extensive uses of aluminum, this point suggests that the Peralta D could be built around a production Maserati. Whether or not that is the case, the mechanical details of the Peralta D are relatively trivial in comparison to the Cu exterior.

#4781. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4780. 6 stellar images of the early universe

Published Oct 25, 2026 8:01 PM EDT

Millions of miles away from Earth, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope are revealing the early days of our vast universe in extraordinary detail. A team at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have developed Lumina, one of the largest and most detailed simulations ever created of the early universe.

The new model is detailed in a study published today in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. It recreates how ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation all interacted during the universe’s first 2 billion years. This gives scientists a new tool to test out their theories about how the cosmos evolved after the big bang. Comparing observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes with Lumina’s predictions, also can help astronomers determine whether their understanding of the laws governing our universe remain accurate or if new discoveries require them to reconsider existing theories.

Creating Lumina required more than 15,000 graphics processing units. Take a peak at some of Lumina’s stellar images and videos in the gallery below. (Click to expand images to full screen.)

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” study lead author Oliver Zier, a computation astronomer and ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, said in a statement. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”

Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulation ever created. This kind of simulation models how the universe’s fundamental ingredients interact to form stars and galaxies. These ingredients include dark matter, light, and gas. Lumina is tracing how the earliest galaxies emerged and transformed the vast regions of gas between them over the universe’s first 2 billion years.

“We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” added Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.”

To view the entire project, visit the Lumina Project.

#4779. Police pull over two men riding an electric couch down the street

Electric scooters have carried just about everything at this point, from commuters and tourists to groceries and probably more than a few ill-advised passengers. But two riders in Charlotte, North Carolina, may have just raised the bar after police stopped them cruising down the street on an actual couch apparently powered by a pair of Lime electric scooters.

Officers with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department encountered the unusual contraption traveling down South Tryon Street, according to a recent post shared by the department.

“Well, this was certainly a first,” police wrote. “Our EDU Officers encountered quite the situation this weekend when they stopped two gentlemen traveling down S. Tryon Street on a couch… Yes, an actual couch.”

From the photo, the setup appears to consist of a full-size sofa perched across two Lime shared electric scooters. Exactly how the scooters were attached – or how steering was accomplished – isn’t clear. But judging by the fact that the riders apparently made it far enough to attract police attention, the system seems to have worked at least reasonably well with some coordinated efforts by the dual pilots.

And frankly, as someone who has famously seen and operated plenty of bizarre electric vehicles over the years, I have to give some points for creativity here.

Police seemed to feel similarly, though they were understandably less enthusiastic about the safety implications of piloting living-room furniture down a public street.

“While we appreciate the creativity, we do have to remind everyone: no matter what you’re ‘driving’ (using that term extremely loosely), please think about safety first,” the department wrote.

If I was a college kid who bought a couch and needed to move it from one apt to another, this is an excellent alternative to carrying it.

Police also joked that it was “probably best to leave the mobile furniture displays to IKEA.”

It isn’t clear whether either rider was cited or arrested, and police didn’t publicly identify the pair.

But while a two-scooter electric couch probably isn’t the micromobility revolution cities had in mind, you’ve got to admit: door-to-door transportation doesn’t get much more comfortable than this.

#4778. In 1934, a doctor brought a dog back to life. He tried to do the same with humans.

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:02 AM EDT

Under the harsh glare of overhead lights at a laboratory at the University of California at Berkeley, Lazarus II lay motionless.

Dr. Robert E. Cornish, who’d asphyxiated the rangy white fox terrier with ether and nitrogen, watched the clock. Six minutes after the final heartbeat, the scientist gathered up the dog and strapped him to a teeterboard, a see-saw-like invention whose back-and-forth, up-and-down motion Cornish believed was key to restoring the blood’s circulation.

He pushed a saline solution primed with oxygen, heart-stimulating adrenalin, and the liver extract heparin into a vein in Lazarus’ thigh, then lowered his head over the patient. As his assistant rocked the teeterboard and rubbed the little body vigorously, Cornish exhaled deep breaths into the dog’s mouth and lungs.

Long seconds turned to minutes and then, suddenly, Lazarus gasped and jerked his leg. Slowly, his heart began to beat. Lazarus II had returned from the dead.

With the invention of modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) still a quarter century off, resurrecting Lazarus after his heart stopped was something of a miracle in 1934. But while the fox terrier lived for another eight hours and 13 minutes, he did not live well, stuck in a restless zombie state punctuated by the occasional whine, bark, and panting.

“Irreversible damage occurs to either the heart or the brain after a period of time, making a good recovery impossible,” Samuel Tisherman, professor of surgery and director for the Center for Critical Care and Trauma Education at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, tells Popular Science.

Lazarus II wasn’t Cornish’s first attempt to revive dying patients using his teeterboard. He wasn’t even the first Lazarus. The young scientist, a former child prodigy who’d earned his doctorate from UC Berkeley at age 22, became obsessed with resuscitation sometime around 1933.

Before working on dogs, Cornish began his reanimating work on people. A 62-year-old printer who died of cardiac arrest was the first to receive Cornish’s reanimation treatment. Four-and-a-half hours after his death, Cornish arrived at the hospital to strap the man’s heating pad-swaddled body to a teeterboard. After see-sawing the patient up and down for 90 minutes, Cornish failed to revive the subject—although Cornish noted a point at which the printer’s “face seemed to warm up suddenly, sparkle returned to the eyes, and soft pulsations were observed in the soft tissue between windpipe and sternum,” according to science journalist Frank Swain’s How to Make a Zombie: The Life (and Death) Science of Reanimation and Mind Control.

Two weeks later, Cornish tried the same treatment on a 22-year-old machinist who’d been pulled dead from the San Francisco Bay three hours before, working his body on the teeterboard for a full four hours. It, too, failed, along with a third attempt the following day in which Cornish submerged an electrocuted cadaver in a warm bath instead of using heating pads before placing the body on the teeterboard.

Dissatisfied with the outcomes, Cornish decided it would be wise to perfect his methodology on fox terriers before returning to human subjects. He named each one Lazarus after the biblical man Jesus brought back to life.

Cornish’s biggest breakthrough came with Lazarus IV. Though blind and unable to stand on its own, within 13 days the dog could crawl, bark, and sit up. Its appetite, too, had returned. Over the few months of his life after death, Lazarus IV went through almost a pound of meat each day.

The next patient, Lazarus V, recovered even more quickly. It took just four days for the dog to resume some normal behaviors despite suffering blindness and brain damage. Like his predecessor, he too lived only a few months.

Despite their mixed outcome, Cornish was praised for his Lazarus experiments. In the press, the scientist who’d often been considered an oddball by his peers for pursuing projects like underwater reading glasses was hailed as a celebrity. A movie about his work, Life Returns, was released in 1935.

But Cornish’s resuscitation experiments were not without controversy. Dogged by animal rights protests and other outcries from the public, UC Berkeley’s administrators had him removed from campus. Cornish continued his work from home, turning a garden shed into a laboratory that neighbors claimed stunk up the street.

The science behind resuscitating a dying patient has come a long way since the Lazarus experiments. These days, “how to restore a pulse depends upon the cause of the cardiac arrest,” says Tisherman.

“The first, most important intervention is assuring good chest compressions,” he continues.

How quickly intervention begins also plays a role. “It’s generally been considered that if the period of no blood flow at all, before someone starts CPR, is greater than five minutes, the outcome will likely be poor,” says Tisherman—though that idea has been challenged and “no one knows for sure.”

While drugs and medications similar to those used by Cornish to improve blood flow and return heart rhythms to normal in his Lazarus experiments play a part in modern resuscitation protocol, emergency medical practitioners have never adopted the teeterboard he believed was key to restoring life.

Cornish never had the opportunity to prove that his teeterboard worked, despite appealing to the governors of Nevada, Arizona, and Colorado for permission to revive criminals executed by the gas chamber shortly after completing his Lazarus experiments. Their refusal didn’t stop Cornish from making one final attempt in 1948, sending multiple requests to the warden at San Quentin State Prison to resuscitate kidnapper and murderer Thomas McMonigle following his upcoming execution by gas chamber—all of which were rebuffed.

Once news of Cornish’s plan for McMonigle became public, more than 50 other “mostly single men” volunteered to be brought back to life by his teeterboard but by then, it seems, Cornish had moved on to something a little less extraordinary: formulating and marketing toothpaste to the American public.

#4777. E-quipment highlight: the highest-rated mowers on Amazon are ELECTRIC (2026)

Despite decades of market dominance, it seems like the days of loud, finicky, gas-powered mowers may finally be behind us; and I say that because – for the second year in a row! – the highest-rated lawnmowers on Amazon won’t burn a drop of gas.

The latest round of dumb oil wars are ratcheting up fuel prices everywhere while, at the same time, state and local governments continue to tightening restrictions on noise and small-engine emissions. Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The good news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer, and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them, electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon, emphatic period, are electric.

In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.

Here’s the rundown, in alphabetical order (by brand).

Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality. The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation.

That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included 56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery, three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.

With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews, the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon. No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.

The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.

For bigger, more demanding lawns, Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries. Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.

WORX’s 40V 17″ Power Share mower is another strong example of how electric lawn care can be both practical and affordable. The WG743 mates a pair of 20V, 4.0 Ah batteries to deliver 40V of power, and those same batteries work across the brand’s broader Power Share lineup of tools – a lineup that includes string trimmers, power drills, and more.

The WORX mower’s standout feature, though, is its “IntelliCut” technology that works a bit like traction control in your car, automatically increasing torque when the mower hits thicker grass (more traction) and backing off when it doesn’t need the extra power (when it detects wheelspin – or, in this case, cutting head spin). Factor in an intentionally lightweight design, seven-position cutting-height adjustment, and the de rigueur options for mulching or bagging, and you’ve got a versatile little mower for keeping a smaller lawn in shape.

Have a Toro 60v mower since 2019 and nothing but superb. Bought a Toro blower which is as powerful then a gas unit. Cleans snow easily off cars, driveways especially powered. My 20 year old skil 18v tools still perform like new with newer higher powered batteries, along with my 20v updated black and decker tool assortment. #4776. The Honda Ridgeline ‘Never Really Started Out to Be a Truck Project’, Designer Says

Plus, a collaboration with Nike was originally on the table.

The Honda Ridgeline has faced ‘fake truck’ accusations for its entire production run. Even after Honda beefed up the model for its second generation, the unibody pickup has never really earned acceptance from the truck community. But the original designer of the Honda Ridgeline said the model was never really supposed to be a pickup in the traditional sense.

“I don’t want to call it a truck because it wasn’t really designed to be a truck, but everybody thinks it is,” Don Herner, a retired Honda designer who worked on the first-generation Ridgeline, said in a video by YouTuber Jack Bontatibus that was brought to broader attention by The Drive.

The video, which features Herner walking around a first-generation Ridgeline, dives deep into the history of Honda’s bedded machine. Herner claims the Ridgeline wasn’t a directive from above, but was instead the result of boredom at Honda’s design studio. After approaching Dave Marek, American Honda’s longtime R&D executive advisor, for permission, Herner and a team of designers began sketching both a mid-size pickup and a compact SUV.

“We started sketching a bunch of different vehicles. And, out of that initial sketch phase, the Ridgeline came out and also the RDX came out of that unplanned, initial impromptu sketch phase,” Herner said in the video. “Eventually one of the market managers came down and was like, ‘Hey Don, what are you guys doing down here?’ So he took all the stuff that we’d done downstairs, brought it upstairs to the executives, and then he kind of got the ball rolling on the executive side.”

The designers had dreamed big, fitting imaginary 35-inch tires and off-road wheels in their sketches. But Honda’s engineering team reportedly had a different idea. Instead of off-road-focused rubber, the engineers wanted to fit smaller wheels and tires—even smaller than the 245mm section tires and 17-inch wheels that the Ridgeline arrived with. And there was a reason for such a departure from the dimensions of a typical mid-size truck.

“This never really started out to be a truck project, per se, because Honda doesn’t make a transmission robust enough to turn gigantic wheels and tires. We were calling it internally the ‘advanced capabilities vehicle,’” Herner explained. “The target for this was, SUV interior size. Our competitors at the time were the [Toyota] Tacoma and a Ford truck...this has a lot more interior space, a lot more legroom, and a lot more couple distance than the Tacoma did at the time.”

Interior packaging was Honda’s biggest focus with the Ridgeline, and Herner said that Honda executives actually examined the interior before the exterior as the Ridgeline got closer to production. Honda wanted as much room as possible inside the Ridgeline, a different approach than the bed-focused design of many older trucks. Speaking of, the first-generation Ridgeline was also criticized for its short, 1100-pound load limit bed—but Herner said the fiberglass bed was meant to take a beating.

“The bed was made to be super, super robust. They overloaded it through computer-aided engineering. .. the entire suspension crushed all the way to the ground and popped back up. The idea was it would survive that kind of a pounding,” Herner said.

Honda even considered partnering with Nike on the project. Herner said that Honda approached Nike’s All Condition Gear (ACG) wing to co-brand the pickup with the footwear brand, and designers even went to Beaverton, Oregon, to visit Nike’s headquarters. Ultimately, the partnership didn’t work out, but the Ridgeline enjoyed a 20-year lifecycle anyway. While production of the second-generation Ridgeline is currently paused, Honda is preparing for a third-generation Ridgeline in 2028 with even more off-road chops.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4775. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4774. Celebrate the flavors of fall with three spicy recipes

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:19 AM EDT

Adapted from Spiced: Recipes Celebrating Spices from Around the World by Priya Mani. (Phaidon, US $54.95, 2026)

Preparation time: 30 minutes, plus 2 hours standing and 8–16 days fermenting

In Korea, families gather each fall (autumn) for kimjang, to make and share large batches of kimchi to sustain them through the winter. This version is classic baechu kimchi made with napa (Chinese) cabbage. Seek out fermented shrimp, saeujeot, at a Korean grocery, while glutinous rice flour, coarse gochugaru flakes, and dashi (powder and concentrate) are available in Asian stores.

Kimchi transforms in flavor and texture as it ferments. Fresh kimchi, baechu geotjeori, is crisp, with a bright gochugaru flavor; it pairs with steamed rice, salads, or bibimbap. After a month, kimchi is sour and piquant; add it to pancakes, kimchijeon, soup, kimchi guk, and Korean Fried Rice (Kimchi-bokkeumbap, page 154). When the kimchi has aged and soured, use it to make rich stews such as kimchi jjigae or mukeunji jjigae, a slow-braised pork stew.

Score the base of the napa (Chinese) cabbage and tear it in half lengthwise. Submerge it in a large bowl of cold water for a few minutes. Remove, and rub the coarse sea salt between the cabbage leaves and set aside to weep in a large bowl for 2 hours; toss the cabbage occasionally.

To make the kimchi paste, whisk the rice flour with the dashi in a small saucepan, making sure there are no lumps. Place it over medium-low heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring constantly until it thickens into a translucent paste. Stir in the sugar, remove from the heat, and let cool for about 15 minutes.

In a blender, combine the cooled paste, garlic, ginger, onion, fish sauce (or soy sauce), and minced fermented shrimp, if using, until smooth. Scoop it into a large bowl, add the gochugaru, Asian pear, scallions (spring onions), radish, and carrot and mix well. This is called yangnyeomjang. Set it aside while you prepare the cabbage.

Drain the cabbage and wash well in multiple changes of cold water. Taste a leaf, it must be well salted and crispy. If it is too salty, let it soak in a bowl of fresh, cold water for 30 minutes more. With very clean hands (or wearing food-grade gloves), spread the yangnyeomjang paste between the cabbage leaves, ensuring an even coating. Fold each half cabbage tightly and pack into suitably sized sterilized glass jars (see page 479). Leave at room temperature for 1–2 days to start fermenting, then store in the refrigerator. For the best flavor, let it ferment for at least 1–2 weeks before eating. Properly stored, kimchi lasts for months in the refrigerator, developing deeper flavors over time.

Cheongyang gochu / C. annuum / 8,000–10,000 SHU

In Korean, gochu simply means chile. Gochugaru, or chile powder specifically used for kimchi, can be milled from several varieties of local chile to suit regional preferences, though the mild, dried, red hong gochu is a good base chile. Another variety, Cheongyang gochu, grown in Cheongyang in South Korea, is a cross with spicy Thai chiles that yields a more pungent product, which can be added to the gochugaru to taste. Red hong gochu are harvested at full maturity, then dehydrated mechanically, but in traditional practice, they are laid out under the clear fall (autumn) sun for several days in a method called taekyung (or taeyangcho). The peppers are then split open and the stems, seeds, and pith are removed, leaving a brilliant red fruit behind. This is milled to produce flakes or a coarse powder, shiny and full of luster. Gochugaru is sold as coarse or finely milled powder.

Preparation time: 15 minutes, plus 3 hours for cooling the rice

Kimchi fried rice is a quick dish to make with matured kimchi. You can use leftover rice, or cook it for the dish as this recipe describes, though as with most fried-rice dishes, day-old rice works best. You can let the rice dry out for a few hours or refrigerate it for the best results. Gochujang is stocked in the Asian pantry aisle of supermarkets.

Cook the rice (see page 479), drizzle with sesame oil, and turn to coat well. Spread the rice out on a baking sheet, cover with a net or cheesecloth (muslin) and dry it out for at least 3 hours or overnight. You can also refrigerate it. The next day, fluff the rice with a fork to separate the grains.

Heat the neutral oil in a large skillet or wok over medium heat. Add the beef or tofu and stir-fry for 8–10 minutes, until well cooked, or the tofu cubes have taken on some color. Increase the heat to medium-high, then toss in the garlic and half the scallions (spring onions), and cook, stirring for 2 minutes, or until fragrant. Add the kimchi and cook for a minute more, stirring occasionally, so it softens and releases its juices. Stir in the gochujang, soy sauce, and sugar and mix well.

Add the rice and toss again until evenly coated. (Add some of the juices from the kimchi jar for some moisture and extra tang to the rice if you like.) Cook for another 3–4 minutes, pressing the rice down so it sizzles and crisps in the oil. Drizzle with sesame oil and mix. Garnish with sesame seeds, seaweed, and the remaining scallion greens. Divide among serving plates and serve with a fried egg on top.

This is a very popular anju, or bar snack, in Korea, served alongside soju or makgeolli.

In a saucepan of salted water, place the tofu, and simmer it over medium heat for about 15 minutes. Remove carefully with a slotted spoon and cut into 1/2-inch (1-cm) thick slices.

Place the kimchi and the remaining ingredients in a mixing bowl (reserving half of the mixed sesame seeds to garnish) and let them marinate for 10 minutes. Transfer to a skillet (frying pan) and bring to a simmer over medium heat. Let the liquids sizzle and nearly evaporate, then turn off the heat.

Arrange the tofu pieces fanned in a ring on a plate. Pour on the warm kimchi mixture, drizzle with more sesame oil to finish, and scatter the scallion (spring onions) greens on top, to serve.

Calabrian Chile Paste / Bomba alla calabrese

Preparation time: 45 minutes, plus 30 hours resting

Bomba alla calabrese is often sold in small jars playfully packed like a “firecracker,” nodding to the condiment’s assertive heat from fresh red, peperoncini a mazzetti chiles. Toss some bomba with pasta, serve it atop bruschetta, or dip your crackers in it—its heat is very moreish, tempting you to dip into it one more time, every time. Chop all the vegetables into 1/4-inch (5-mm) dice.

Place the eggplant (aubergine), bell pepper, celery, and carrot in a large bowl.

Rinse the basil leaves and pat them dry with a paper towel.

In a large mixing bowl, sprinkle coarse salt at the bottom, then add alternating layers of vegetables and basil, generously sprinkling salt between the layers. Cover with a plate, place a heavy weight, such as a small stone mortar on top, and let it rest for 24 hours.

Meanwhile, place the chopped peperoncini chiles in a separate bowl and add 1/4 teaspoon of coarse salt. Wearing food-safe gloves, massage well, then cover with plastic wrap (clingfilm) and let stand alongside the salted vegetables.

After 24 hours, squeeze the vegetables thoroughly to remove as much liquid as possible. A potato ricer or sieve works well for this step. Transfer the drained vegetables to a clean, non- reactive bowl (like glass), add the vinegar, cover, and let it rest for 6 hours. Then, squeeze them again to remove the excess vinegar.

Place the drained vegetables and salted peperoncini in a food processor and pulse in short bursts until coarsely chopped, avoiding making a smooth purée. Add the garlic and anchovies, if using, then taste to check if the salting is optimal. The condiment’s flavor has not yet developed, this is just to ensure it is not too salty. I like to add the briny liquid from the peperoncini to retain its burn, but you can skip it to moderate the heat level.

Spoon the mixture into sterilized glass jars (see page 479), leaving space at the top. Pour enough olive oil to cover the vegetables completely, then seal the jars tightly. Store in a cool, dark place for up to a month. The condiment will mellow and become very flavorful as it sits in the spices and aromatics for a week. After opening and using, always push down any vegetable matter from the sides and top off with more olive oil to keep the surface sealed from air.

Peperoncini a mazzetti / C. annuum / 15,000–30,000 SHU

In Calabria, at the toe of the Italian peninsula, flanked by the Ionian Sea to the east and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west, hot, dry winds sear over the Calabrian coast from North Africa. Many feisty chiles thrive in the region’s clay soil, the spirit of many of Italy’s iconic condiments including ’nduja, sardella, and bomba alla Calabrese. Peperoncini a mazzetti are a local Calabrian chile pepper whose fruits grow in tight clusters (mazzetti means “little bunches”). Because of their curious appearance, many gardeners grow them as decorative plants as well as for culinary use. They tend to be pungent but not excessively fiery, with a fairly direct chile heat that works well fresh, cooked, or dried. They are sold in bundles, fresh or sun-dried, still perched on their stems. A crisp green chile with nearly no heat also goes by the name peperoncini (or frigitelli or Campanian friarelli peppers). In Italy, they are served pan-fried as a snack with a little salt.

Priya Mani is a food-historian, award-winning writer, and designer leading research-driven projects on ingredients, flavor, and material culture. She founded Appetite Studio, based in Copenhagen, and is the author of, and contributor to, several food books  articles for the BBC, and journals, including Bloomsbury Handbook of Indian Cuisine (Bloomsbury Academic, 2023). In 2022 she won the prestigious Guild of Food Writers Award (2022) and the International Association for Culinary Professionals (IACP) award. She   is a trustee of the Oxford Food Symposium, and  a director at the  British Guild of Food Writers, leading the committee on Diversity.

#4773. Battery electric, solar-powered reefer units reach their first customers

The first regular production solar-powered electric trailer refrigeration unit (TRU) in Australia has hit the road with a real customer. Family-owned transport giant Wickham Freight Lines took delivery of the revolutionary reefer just this week.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike, and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.

After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines. “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

Solar powered refrigeration truck looks like a natural combination. Cost of the solar is offset somewhat by not needing diesel tank, motor, and generator. Majority of savings probably come form not needing constant refueling (fuel + labor), or in not needing to overhaul the engine periodically.

I would be very interested in knowing how quickly the system pays for itself.

#4772. XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]

The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification. It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it, and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn. “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in (I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot, yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage. Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them.

It doesn’t have to be autonomous because it’s electric it only needs to be powered by electric motors not gas to be better in every way.

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

#4771. Family finds World War II grenade in grandfather’s basement

Published Oct 26, 2026 10:57 AM EDT

A family near Kalamazoo, Michagan was in for a surprise while cleaning out their grandfather’s basement. Amid the dusty storeroom clutter, the Paw Paw Township residents discovered a vintage, possibly live grenade from World War II apparently forgotten after decades in storage. Unsure what to do with their newfound, potentially deadly device, family members quickly contacted local emergency services.

According to the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office, first responders confirmed the grenade’s authenticity and estimated that it dates back to 1945. However, they couldn’t immediately determine if the weapon remained functional after more than 80 years tucked away in the cellar. For that, officials needed to call in the Kalamazoo Department of Public Safety Bomb Squad.

Peering inside the grenade required specially designed X-ray equipment, which lets explosives experts examine internal components from a safe distance before handling the weapon. Thankfully, the process remained relatively straightforward and the team confirmed that the veteran wasn’t a reckless wartime collector—someone already had decommissioned the grenade long ago. That doesn’t let history buffs off the hook, however.

“The Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office reminds residents that old military ordnance, ammunition, and other potentially explosive devices can remain dangerous for decades, regardless of their age or appearance,” officials cautioned.

Unexpected, military-grade finds are more common than it may seem. Recently, a late WWII veteran’s neighbors located a trove of files related to Stalag Luft 3, the infamous Nazi prison camp depicted in The Great Escape. Researchers are regularly rediscovering long-lost shipwrecks from the era, while restoration specialists are even bringing vintage aircraft back to life.

First responders also offered some standard guidelines for anyone else who might stumble across unexpected incendiary devices, but they all basically boil down to one simple rule: do not mess with them. Any suspected explosives—no matter how old—should always be handled by trained professionals, so it’s best to immediately retreat to a safe distance and call the proper authorities.

“Even items believed to be military souvenirs or decommissioned equipment should be treated as potentially hazardous until examined by qualified professionals,” the sheriff’s office added.

#4770. McLaren’s Next Supercar Will Be Named ‘McL 820,’ Arrive in 2027 [Updated]

The company teased the name in the traditional way: by writing it on a giant kiwi.

Update, 1:45 p.m. October 30th: McLaren has confirmed in a statement that ‘McL 820’ will be the name of its next supercar, due in 2027, and also confirmed its 820 metric horsepower output. The company has also provided us pictures of the giant kiwi statue referred to below.

McLaren Automotive as we know it—i.e. the company that began with the MP4-12C—is marking its 16th year in existence here in 2026, and like many a teenager, it’s in the process of reinventing itself. Being a corporation, however, its options for dying its hair, changing its wardrobe, or “discovering” how awesome Dark Side of the Moon is are rather limited. So instead, McLaren is shaking up its design language, bringing in new investment, and adding more models, including an SUV. And, it seems, changing up its nomenclature.

The initial evidence came with the McL 6GT showcased at this year’s Monterey Car Week, a distinctly (and unusually, for the brand) retro-inspired hypercar with an honest-to-God manual gearbox. Now, the folks at Britain’s Autocar have come across evidence that the next car to join the company’s lineup could also use the nomenclature defined by that Pebble Beach reveal. More specifically, that it may be called the McL 820.

Naturally, Autocar learned this via a giant kiwi.

Not the tartly delicious fruit, of course; that would be absurd. No, the bird—the one endemic to founder Bruce McLaren’s native New Zealand. The “Speedy Kiwi” logo has long been part of the company’s culture, and the brand is in the midst of trying to build awareness of it, as the recent Instagram post below shows.

Another part of that promotion, according to Autocar, involved the erection of a massive statue (well, massive relative to an actual kiwi) of the bird in London’s Covent Garden neighborhood on Thursday, complete with natty black-and-orange livery. Hidden away on its flank is an alphanumeric code: McL 820.

That alone doesn’t officially mean anything, but a bit of deductive reasoning leads to a specific conclusion. Fact: the McL 6GT shows McLaren is now using the “McL” nomenclature. Fact: the company has announced its core 720S / 750S line of supercars is concluding production. Fact: the numbers in those names refer to the models’ output in metric horsepower. Fact: the company has never rolled out a new production model that was less powerful than its predecessor. Ergo, “McL 820” would be a highly logical name for a new generation of McLaren supercar.

Furthering the evidence: an output of 820 metric ponies would equate to roughly 810 imperial horses, which just so happens to be what McLaren dealers said would be the power generated by a forthcoming mid-engined supercar that supposedly goes by the internal code of “P34.” That car was somewhat oddly described as slotting between the current Artura and 750S in terms of price and positioning, generating its power from a hybrid twin-turbo V-6 rather than the new generation of V-8 the company is supposedly working on. If true, that suggests that the “true” 720S / 750S replacement would likely push closer to 1000 horses, making it a proper Lamborghini Revuelto rival ... with, presumably, a board-pleasing pricetag to match.

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. A 12-year veteran of journalism, he formerly worked at Gear Patrol, The Drive, and RIDES Magazine, and contributed to the New York Daily News and Jalopnik, among other outlets. You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

#4769. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4768. Earth’s first fully-marine amphibian stalked the seafloor with a chunky, bony body

Published Oct 26, 2026 12:00 PM EDT

Nearly 237 million years ago, a spiky and toothy bottom dweller skulked the Late Triassic oceans that once covered present-day China. What sets this newly discovered giant salamander-sized prehistoric amphibian apart is not its impressive body–it’s that it lived in the ocean. The newly described Gerrothorax maritimus is the first example of a fully marine amphibian in the fossil record, according to a study published today in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

There are currently over 8,000 species of living amphibians, and none have been known to live in fully marine (salt water) environments. Less than two percent like crab-eating frogs (Fejervarya cancrivora) and some spotted salamandars have any degree of salt tolerance. Other four-limbed animals, including birds, reptiles, and mammals, all have species who can survive without any food or water from land. There was also no evidence of a fully marine amphibian in the fossil record. Until now.

In this study, a team from the University of California, Davis in the United States and Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou in China analyzed two nearly complete skeletons found in southern China’s Guizhou Province. The fossils were found in an area once covered by ocean and hundreds of miles from any large land mass.

“This area is part of an ecosystem that we’ve been looking at and trying to reconstruct,” Ryosuke Motani, a study co-author and paleontologist at UC Davis, said in a statement. “We’ve been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian and it’s a sort of very unusual member of the lineage.”

The well-preserved skeletons helped the team reconstruct what Gerrothorax maritimus looked like and offer clues to its marine life. Notably, it had a flattened body covered in bony armor. This armor likely defended it against predators like the 10-foot-long ichthyosaur that stalked these seas millions of years ago. Gerrothorax maritimus itself was roughly three feet long with a disc-shaped body.

“If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s big,” Motani said. “It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”

Based on Gerrothorax maritimus’  bony armor and the shape of its skull, the team believes that it was a bottom-dwelling suction feeder, similar to the wobbegong, a family of 12 bottom-dwelling carpet shark species alive today.

“They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” said Motanti.

Modern amphibians can’t live in marine environments because their skin does not tolerate salt. The skin is permeable, and allows them to use it for multiple purposes like respiration. Amphibians don’t drink or breathe through the same mouth opening since they can do both just using their skin.

Due to this salt-intolerant biology, they must live in or near freshwater. While some modern species like the crab-eating frog have some degree of salt tolerance, they will lose weight in brackish waters and must recover in freshwater.

The researchers propose that bony armor and a more fish-like body helped Gerrothorax maritimus circumvent this limitation. The armor would have kept its skin from absorbing water, meaning that it needed to drink salt water with its mouth, and then absorb it through its digestive tract. The creature’s gills would have allowed it to filter out the salt. Other species in the Gerrothorax also have gills.

According to the team, the fossils’ location within deep sea sediments and the fact that they were nearly complete led them to believe that Gerrothorax maritimus was an ocean-dweller.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” said Motani. “But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”

#4767. Texas Police Are Keeping the Public Safe With a 710-HP Dodge Durango SRT Hellcat

Everything is bigger in Texas—including, it seems, the amount of horsepower needed to serve and protect.

Texas is the biggest state in the lower 48. From its chicken-fried steaks to its Buc-ee's travel centers, the Lone Star State takes advantage of all that space by making everything bigger than you might expect. Now, the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) is getting in on the act: The DPS’s North Texas Region recently announced on Facebook that a Dodge Durango SRT Hellcat will be joining its fleet. Because in Texas, a 710-horsepower police SUV is completely reasonable.

The Texas DPS didn't go into much detail about how the Durango SRT Hellcat would be deployed. It simply said: "All that horsepower. One mission: Public Safety." That mission apparently calls for an SUV with a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 under the hood. With a top speed of 180 miles per hour, the Durango SRT Hellcat can cover a lot of ground quickly, and in an emergency, every second counts.

Of course, top speed is only one part of the equation. If the Texas DPS ever finds itself considering a PIT maneuver on a Texas-sized pickup truck, having roughly 5600 pounds of SUV at its disposal might be reassuring. Whether putting an $80,000 Hellcat through that kind of punishment is a good idea is another question entirely.

There is one thing the Texas DPS will need to keep in mind if it intends to use the Durango SRT Hellcat in highway pursuits: range. The EPA rates the supercharged SUV at just 14 miles per gallon combined, and that figure is likely to be far lower when the V-8 is in maximum attack mode. (Our testing saw just 10.7 mpg in the significantly less powerful 2026 Durango R/T 392, for reference.)

Whether this Durango will spend its days chasing bad guys or simply making appearances at community events remains to be seen. (Road & Track has reached out to the Texas DPS for comment, but did not hear back by the time of publication.) But no matter how it is used, it’s certainly going to attract plenty of attention. And while a Hellcat might seem excessive for a police vehicle ... this is Texas we're talking about.

#4766. The 2026 Mama Bear Award goes to a black bear with a mullet

Published Oct 26, 2026 1:08 PM EDT

While Fat Bear Week has come and gone, there is another group of Alaskan bears currently getting their due. The United States Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in southeastern Alaska.

Tongass is the nation’s largest national forest and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. It is home to Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, which is home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, there are 39 known bears that feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. Thirty-one are black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight are brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their counterparts further to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return here every summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Osso! The adult female black bear was first spotted in 2022 and has a white chest patch shaped like the letter I. She usually has a mullet of hair on the top of her head at the end of the summer season. Her name is spelled either Osso (Italian for bone), because her chest patch also resembles a bone or Oso (Spanish for bear). She had one cub in 2019, two in 2024, and three this year.

Mother bears show fearless aggression when sensing any danger to their young, and the Forest Service says Osso is a prime example of this tenacity.

“Feeding and watching out for three cubs was more than a full-time job, especially with so many other bears about,” the team writes. “Scuba Sue, a female brown bear, got too close for comfort on this occasion and Osso didn’t hesitate before sending her cubs up a tree and taking a swipe at Sue. Not all heroes wear capes, some pop their jaws and raise their claws.”

Unfortunately, Osso was only seen with two cubs in August. While it is not clear what happened to her third cub, the Forest Service assumes she did her best to protect the cubs.
